lines: Factorial decomposition of evaluation variance has roots in the ML reproducibility literature. \citet{bouthillier2021accounting} introduced an ANOVA-based template that decomposes benchmark variance across implementation details, hyperparameters, and data splits, establishing that design choices account for a substantial share of reproducibility failures. Subsequent studies applied similar decomposition to specific evaluation facets \citep{dodge2020finetuning, henderson2018deep, magnusson2023reproducibility}. \citet{messing2026hidden} brought Generalizability theory into LLM evaluation, decomposing variance across five methodology facets on a single benchmark (judge identity: 43.8\%; see Positioning below for detailed comparison). \citet{madaan2024quantifying} proposed per-factor variance metrics for LLM evaluation benchmarks but did not cross factors simultaneously. Holistic evaluation frameworks \citep{liang2023helm, kiela2021dynabench} standardize multi-scenario comparison but do not decompose variance sources. \citet{blackwell2024towards} quantified uncertainty in benchmark scores, and \citet{qian2026benchmark} conducted systematic meta-evaluation of LLM benchmarks; \citet{burnell2023rethink} called for rethinking evaluation reporting standards; \citet{saxon2024metrology} advocated model metrology as a framework for rigorous benchmark design. Recently, G-theory has been applied to LLM-based writing assessment \citep{wei2025gtheory} and annotation reliability \citep{varannot2025gtheory}, but these studies address scoring consistency rather than benchmark evaluation variance. \citet{kunievsky2025intent} proposed an alternative decomposition that separates intent uncertainty, articulation variance, and model uncertainty, but this framework does not cross infrastructure and methodology facets in a factorial design.
